data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI arises primarily from the slow release of sensible heat stored during the day in high-thermal-mass urban materials (concrete, asphalt); the cross-city gap is largest where nighttime cooling rates are slowest, which scales with urban thermal mass and impervious surface fraction.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If rural and urban cooling rates after sunset are measured to be equal, the thermal-mass-release mechanism is falsified.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the nocturnal UHI is observed to be stronger in cities with low building density and high sky view factor, this mechanism is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If daytime heat storage is not substantially greater in cities than in their surroundings, the mechanism fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"During the day, dense urban materials with high heat capacity and low albedo absorb large amounts of solar energy. After sunset, the countryside cools rapidly via longwave radiative loss to the sky, but urban surfaces release their stored sensible heat slowly, keeping the air warmer. Cities with more impervious surface and thermal mass retain more daytime storage and cool more slowly, producing a larger nocturnal gap.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
